q: Your program asks for memory with p = malloc(1000). Why should the very next line check p?
choices: It returns NULL when memory runs out
It can return a negative number
explain: When the system can't give the memory, malloc returns NULL, a pointer to nothing. Writing through NULL crashes the program, or on some systems corrupts memory silently. Check right away: if (!p) { perror("malloc"); exit(1); }. malloc never returns a size or a negative number, only an address or NULL.

q: You open a C program you have never seen. Which function runs first?
explain: Every C program starts in the function called main; the others only run when main (or a function it calls) calls them. It is written int main(void), or int main(int argc, char **argv) to receive the command-line arguments. Reading a new program? Start at main.

q: You wrote hello.c. How do you turn it into a program you can run, with gcc?
explain: gcc hello.c translates the C code into machine code; -o hello names the result hello (without it you get a file called a.out). Then ./hello runs it: the ./ says 'the one in this folder'. make is another tool that reads a Makefile, it doesn't take a .c file like this.

q: C has no string type, only arrays of characters. How does a function know where the text ends?
explain: A C string ends with a zero byte, written '\0', stored right after the last letter. strlen, printf("%s") and friends read until they meet it. So "hi" takes 3 bytes. Forget the zero byte and they keep reading past your text into whatever memory comes next.

q: A program declares `int *p;`. What kind of variable is p?
explain: The * in a declaration means pointer: p holds the address of an int somewhere in memory, not an int itself. Later, *p (with the star in an expression) means 'the int at that address': x = *p reads it, *p = 5 changes it. An array of ints would be written int a[10].

q: In C, what do you get when you write `&x` in front of a variable x?
explain: & gives the address where x is stored in memory. That is what you put in a pointer: int *p = &x;. It is how a function can change your variable: scanf("%d", &x) receives the address, so it can write into x. It is not a copy of x.

q: Your C program needs memory whose size is only known while it runs. Which function asks for it?
explain: malloc(size) reserves that many bytes on the heap, memory that stays until you give it back. Every malloc needs a matching free(p) once you're done, otherwise the program leaks memory and grows over time. new belongs to C++, not C.

q: Most C files start with lines like `#include <stdio.h>`. What does that line do?
choices: Imports a module at run time
explain: Before compiling, the preprocessor replaces the #include line with the whole content of that header file. stdio.h describes printf and friends, so the compiler knows how to call them. The code of printf itself is added later, when the program is linked.

q: Your program ends with `return 0;` in main. What does that 0 tell whoever ran it?
explain: The value main returns becomes the program's exit code: 0 means success, any other number an error. The shell shows it with echo $?, and scripts use it (./prog && echo ok). Return 1 when something went wrong, so scripts can notice.

q: gcc builds your code without a word, yet it has bugs. Which option makes gcc point out the usual mistakes?
explain: -Wall turns on the common warnings: a variable used before it gets a value, a wrong printf format, a comparison that is always true. Add -Wextra for more. A warning is often a real bug, so fix them all. -O2 is about speed, not warnings.

q: Your program stops with 'Segmentation fault'. What happened?
choices: Touching memory you're not allowed to
explain: The program touched memory it doesn't own, and the system stopped it. Usual causes: using a NULL pointer, reading past the end of an array, or using memory after free. Build with -g -fsanitize=address and run it again: it shows the exact line.

q: A bug makes your program call free(p) twice on the same pointer. What happens?
choices: The memory is freed twice as fast
explain: The second free hands back memory that may already belong to something else: this is undefined behavior. It may crash, silently corrupt data, or even be used by an attacker. The compiler can't see it. Habit: write p = NULL; right after free(p), since free(NULL) does nothing.

q: Why is `gets()` banned?
choices: It can't limit the input size: buffer overflow
explain: gets(buf) reads a whole line into buf without knowing how big buf is. A longer line writes past the end, over other variables: a buffer overflow, a classic way to take control of a program. It was removed from the language. fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin) stops at the size you give.

q: In a C file, a function is declared `static int helper(void)`. What does static change?
choices: Keeps it private to its file
explain: On a function, static makes it visible only inside its own .c file: other files can't call it, and its name can't clash with theirs. Use it for helpers. On a variable inside a function, static means something else: it keeps its value from one call to the next.

q: Why is `printf(user_input)` dangerous?
choices: %x and %n in the input read and write memory
explain: printf treats its first argument as a format. If a user types %x %x, printf reads values off the stack and shows them; %n even writes to memory. That is a format string bug. Always write printf("%s", user_input): the input is then only text. gcc -Wformat-security warns about it.

q: Your C program sometimes crashes, sometimes not. Which tool watches its memory use while it runs?
explain: valgrind ./prog runs the program in a checker that reports reads past an array, use after free, and leaks, with the line numbers. Another way: compile with -fsanitize=address (AddressSanitizer), which is faster. gdb shows where it crashed, not the bad access that came before.

q: What can go wrong in `malloc(count * size)` when count comes from input?
choices: The product overflows and too little is allocated
explain: Numbers in C have a maximum. A huge count times size wraps around to a small number, so malloc reserves a small block. The program then writes count items into it and runs past the end: a buffer overflow. calloc(count, size) checks the multiplication and fails cleanly instead.

q: A header file starts with #ifndef CONFIG_H / #define CONFIG_H. What is this 'header guard' for?
explain: In a big project, the same header often gets included twice through other headers, and defining the same struct twice is an error. The first time, CONFIG_H is not defined: the content is used and CONFIG_H gets defined. The second time it's skipped. #pragma once does the same in one line.

q: You run ./prog input.txt. In main(int argc, char **argv), what is in argv[0]?
explain: argv[0] is the program's name as it was typed: ./prog. The real arguments start at argv[1], here input.txt, and argc counts everything, so argc is 2. Classic bug: reading argv[1] without checking argc first, which crashes when no argument is given.

q: A project says 'just run make'. Which file does make read to know what to build?
explain: make reads a Makefile in the current folder. Each rule says target: files it depends on, then the commands on lines that start with a tab (not spaces). make only rebuilds what changed since last time. CMake and Ninja are other tools, with their own files.

q: gcc main.c -o app stops with: undefined reference to `mean'. mean() is written in stats.c. What went wrong?
choices: The linker was never given stats.c
explain: undefined reference comes from the linker, the last step of gcc: main.c calls mean(), but only stats.c holds its code, and gcc wasn't given it. List every .c file: gcc main.c stats.c -o app. The .h file only promises that mean() exists somewhere.

q: gcc -Wall says: suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value, on if (x = 0). What is the real bug?
choices: = stores 0 in x; the test wanted ==
The if needs extra parentheses to compile
x must be declared before the if
explain: = stores a value, == compares. if (x = 0) puts 0 in x and the test is always false; if (x = 5) is always true. gcc builds it anyway, so without -Wall the bug is silent. Build with -Wall and treat each warning as a possible bug.

q: Your C program says only 'Segmentation fault'. What does building it with gcc -g change?
choices: It keeps line numbers: a debugger shows where it died
It makes gcc stop at the first error
explain: -g adds debug information to the program: file names, line numbers, variable names. The program runs the same, but gdb (or AddressSanitizer) can now tell you the exact line: gcc -g prog.c -o prog && gdb -q ./prog, then run and bt.

q: Your program crashed inside gdb. Which command shows the chain of calls that led to the crash?
explain: bt (backtrace) lists the calls, the one that crashed first: #0 is where it died, #1 who called it, and so on, each with its file and line. next runs one line, list shows source code, info registers shows raw CPU values.

q: In gdb, print total says <optimized out>. The program was built with gcc -O2 -g. What helps?
choices: Add more printf calls in gdb
explain: -O2 lets gcc move code around and keep values only in registers, so some variables vanish and lines run out of order. For debugging, build with -Og (or -O0) and -g: the program follows your code line by line. Release builds keep -O2.

q: A loop runs 10,000 times and fails on one item. What does break f if id == 42 do in gdb?
choices: It stops in f only when id is 42
It sets id to 42 when f starts
explain: A conditional breakpoint stops only when its condition is true, so you skip the 9,999 good passes. Then print shows the variables and next steps through. Without the condition you'd type continue thousands of times.

q: gcc area.c -o area fails: undefined reference to `sqrt'. area.c includes <math.h>. What fixes it?
choices: Add -lm at the end: gcc area.c -o area -lm
explain: <math.h> only declares sqrt; its code is in the maths library, libm, which gcc doesn't link by default on Linux. -lm links it; put it after your files, since the linker reads left to right. The header and the library are two different things.

q: A modern C project has CMakeLists.txt or meson.build instead of a hand-written Makefile. What do CMake and Meson do?
choices: They generate the build files for a tool like Ninja or make
explain: CMake and Meson describe the project once (sources, libraries, options) and generate what actually runs the build, often Ninja, which is fast. The compiler is still gcc or clang. Typical: meson setup build && ninja -C build, or cmake -B build && cmake --build build.
